# IPsec Ownership and IPv4 Selection Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally started from two related terms in reports: IPsec interface ownership and IPv4 address selection. Early troubleshooting typically treated them as a single line of investigation. On seeing an interface name, people would look for the corresponding IPv4; on seeing IPv4 change, they would first suspect that interface ownership had changed. Some people were still using this entry point while 2026.09 was being closed out, so the old assessments were not removed from the page.

Here, "interface ownership" refers to the IPsec interface clue recorded during a forwarding-policy or session assessment; "IPv4 address selection" refers to the IPv4 result selected during the same kind of troubleshooting. Both may appear in a single report, or only one may appear. The old page did not require them to come from the same observation, so "both terms have appeared" was often written as "a change in one caused a change in the other".

## Old entry point

The earliest field records contained only this tree, and the actions were straightforward. It is retained because historical reports still describe things in this order:

```text
An anomaly in IPv4 address selection occurs
|
+-- Is the IPsec interface name visible?
|   |
|   +-- Yes: Confirm the IPv4 corresponding to that interface; if inconsistent, consider ownership no longer valid
|   `-- No: Infer the interface from the selected IPv4; if it cannot be inferred, consider there to be no usable ownership
|
`-- Has IPv4 remained unchanged?
    |
    +-- Yes: Take no action for now
    `-- No: Check address selection first, then the interface
```

The advantage of this tree is that very little information needs to be recorded. Troubleshooting can continue with just one interface name or one IPv4 from the field. This is also its problem: when the interface name is missing, address selection is forced to serve as an identity clue; when the address changes, the old interpretation becomes "ownership is no longer valid"; when the address remains unchanged for the time being, interface-side anomalies are easily reduced to "take no action for now". In the old context of this page, "no usable ownership" is a classification reached at the end of a branch, not a verified runtime result.

The early records also required looking at the selection result first, then deciding whether to continue examining the interface. They did not specify where the selection result came from, nor did they require the interface name and IPv4 to appear in the same observation window. As a result, a field case with only a snippet of address records would be expanded into a seemingly complete explanation: the address can be selected, so interface ownership must exist; the address changed, so interface ownership must have changed. This inference remains on the old page and must not be treated as a newly confirmed result.

## What to record during review

The later addendum did not rewrite the old tree; instead, it added the information that needs to be kept side by side. First, record the interface side: whether the IPsec interface name appeared verbatim in the report. Then record the address side: what IPv4 was actually selected at the time. Finally, record the rule side: which category of routing priority was being examined. If all three come from the same field case, they can be put in one record; if their sources are unclear, record them separately.

If the interface side is empty, you can only say that the current material contains no interface name, not fill that in as "there is no interface". If the address side is empty, you can only say that no IPv4 selection result was recorded, not infer that the address was not selected. If both appear but their chronological order is unclear, the old tree can still be used to choose the next step, but the two must not be combined into a causal relationship asserted to have occurred. In particular, do not use IPv4 from historical records to replace the interface name missing from a new field case.

When the following combinations occur, branch according to what is actually present:

```text
Both the interface name + IPv4 are present
├─ Confirmed to be from the same observation
│  ├─ Record the interface name and address
│  └─ Then identify the rule category being examined
└─ Source or order is unclear
   └─ Keep the two items separate, stopping with the association unconfirmed

Only IPv4 is present
├─ There is an explicit address selection result
│  └─ Record the address, without inferring the interface from it
└─ There is only a description of an "address anomaly"
   └─ Stop, do not adjust rule priorities

Only the IPsec interface name is present
├─ It comes from this field case
│  └─ Record the interface and wait for the address-side result
└─ It comes only from an old record
   └─ Do not merge it with the new address
```

The stopping conditions here do not mean that recording is allowed only after all the material has been gathered; they prevent one field from supplying a conclusion for another. The two observations can be kept side by side; a stable address-to-interface mapping must not be established merely because their names are similar, or because both appeared on two cards.

## Routing file entry point

A nearby reference point is `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/routing.rs`. Four priority constants appear at the beginning of the file: `RULE_PRIORITY_DAEMON_BASE`, `RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_BASE`, `RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_FALLBACK_BASE`, and `RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_DISABLE_SYSTEM_BASE`. Their corresponding values, in order, are 20600, 20700, 20800, and 20900. After opening the file, first confirm whether the observation at hand corresponds to the daemon, upstream, fallback, or disable-system rule category; do not default to upstream rules just because there is an address anomaly.

The same file also lists `IpOperation`, `IpFamily`, and `RouteType`. These are useful starting points when reading the code, but type names cannot supply concrete operations missing from the field evidence. The file header directly imports `HashSet`, `io`, `IpAddr`, `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr`, and `Ipv4Inet`. These names show that address, IPv4 subnet, and collection handling appear near one another within this file's local scope; by themselves, they do not record the final ownership of any particular IPsec interface.

If the old troubleshooting process went directly from "the wrong address was selected" to upstream rules, then inferred the interface from those rules, first return to the constant names and field records. The four constants can identify the rule category being examined, but cannot fill in a missing interface name, IPv4, or observation order. The old version described looking at the address first and then the interface as a recovery path; this action can still explain why the investigation entered this file at the time, but it cannot justify changing the rule category.

## Two types of field records

**The interface still appears, but IPv4 is unstable.** The old tree would lead to "ownership is no longer valid". The review record can retain this old assessment while recording the observed facts as "the interface side is present, and the address side has changed". Without the rule category and chronological order from the same observation, this must not be extended to a particular priority range. The address change is a result observed in this field case; it does not mean that interface ownership has changed.

**IPv4 is reported, but the interface name is missing.** The old tree would infer the interface from the address and write "no usable ownership" if the inference failed. This path explains why historical records lack interface names, but if the inferred name comes only from another record, do not merge it into the current field case. The presence of an address only shows that an address-side result was recorded; the interface side remains empty.

**Both the interface name and IPv4 are present, but their order of appearance is unclear.** Such records appear complete on the surface, but are actually more prone to being combined incorrectly. First note that both items have appeared, then note that their order is unconfirmed. Whether the interface name appeared before or after the address was selected, or came from another round of observation, should remain a question mark if it was not recorded; do not substitute "the two terms appeared together" for the order of events.

## Card addenda

The historical description of VPN-212 only states that existing calls preserve IPsec interface ownership; it does not provide a complete IPv4 selection process. It can serve as an interface-side entry point, but cannot replace a specific field case. VPN-224 describes the issue as an anomaly in a specific way of using IPv4 address selection, and asks for a case in the repository that still relies on that behavior, with the rule file location and final list of findings recorded. It is suitable for supplementing address-side records, but should not be used in reverse to prove that interface ownership has changed.

VPN-212 was later handled by the current on-call person, with the recorded reason that the previous owner was not in the current cycle. This change explains why the old entry point continued to be used, but adds no address selection evidence. On this page, the two cards are used only to separate the interface-side description from the address-side field case still to be supplied. For malformed tunnel record framing, go to DOC-20; do not incorporate tunnel record format anomalies into this page's branches.

## Old recommendations and unresolved points

Three statements in the old recommendations need to be understood as written in their historical context: "the selected IPv4 is evidence of ownership", "an address change equals an ownership change", and "if the interface is not visible, infer it from the address". They explain how early troubleshooting converged quickly, and are precisely why this page was later retained as an old entry point. The review only added requirements to record the interface, address, rule category, and order; it did not add a reproducible call chain to this page, so new wording must not be used to repackage the old assessments as established conclusions.

Still unresolved: the specific way of using IPv4 address selection has not yet been documented here as a call sequence; there are insufficient records to determine whether the IPsec interface ownership preserved by existing calls is at the same rule stage as address selection; and no material on this page establishes a stable address-to-interface mapping. If the next field investigation is to continue using this page, first record the interface name, IPv4, the rule category, and the observation order, then decide whether to enter a specific branch in the routing file.

# Malformed tunnel record compatibility workflow

The original notes put "malformed tunnel record framing" and neighbour state in the same place solely because the issue name and call name from the old investigation both led to `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/neighbour.rs`. That investigation had not followed the caller's directories all the way through, so the old entry was easy to read as "framing is handled in neighbour.rs". That statement is still retained because many old links use it for navigation; it is not a final ownership determination.

## What the old entry point is still useful for

`neighbour.rs` is not a useless stopping point. The dependencies listed at the top of the file are enough to help distinguish several scenarios:

- `std::collections::HashMap` is a reminder to first check whether the record is staged in a key-value container, rather than passing the next chunk of bytes directly to the parser;
- `std::io` is where the original read/write error context needs to be preserved;
- `std::net::IpAddr` indicates that this adjacency code touches address objects; address conversion failures must not be conflated with record boundaries;
- `futures_util::TryStreamExt` requires checking whether the async stream stops at `next`, on an error, or at end of stream.

These only indicate the order of inspection; they do not mean that all four are involved in handling malformed records. This is where the old notes kept expanding their claims: after seeing streaming dependencies, they combined "end of stream" and "incomplete record" into a single conclusion. The follow-up review did not support that conflation.

## Moving away from the old directory

The directory structure supplied by the caller is a more reliable starting point for this round. When reproducing the issue, start by following the caller's directories and note three things at the stopping point: the call site, the object obtained, and the reason for stopping. The object may be an input fragment, address state, or a stream item; do not call all of them tunnel records up front. Only include a level in the new entry point for framing if record boundaries are actually visible at that level.

If the traversal reaches `neighbour.rs`, first check whether it is handling netlink neighbour state or merely waiting for upstream to provide the next item. The former should stay in the neighbour-state investigation; only in the latter case should you continue tracing toward the read or conversion step. The goal is not to split modules into tiny pieces, but to avoid labeling addresses, caching, and stream termination as the same fault because of one malformed input.

The to-do for VPN-214 requires reproducing this behavior from the directory structure supplied by the caller and confirming the actual path where traversal stops. The card is only an entry point; this page preserves the old paths and changes in assessment during the migration.

## Restoring the old path

If the new traversal has not reached a specific handling point, do not remove the old navigation to `neighbour.rs`. Label it "old entry point located by issue name and call name" and add this run's stopping point alongside it. That way, you can still get in through historical links next time without making an unconfirmed path look like a completed migration.

If the evidence only shows a stop on the `TryStreamExt` side, with no record boundary, error context, or caller object, restore the old entry point and do not move framing to the read layer yet. Conversely, if the caller can consistently provide a complete object and it is truncated at the next level, add the new path to this page and keep the old entry point with an explanation of why it was replaced.

DOC-21 is the archived history of the rolled-back neighbour-state trial run. It has no current acceptance items and cannot substitute for confirming the malformed tunnel record path.

# Compatibility Workflow for Malformed Tunnel Records

This entry is still referenced by old links, so the earliest location guidance has not been removed. The earliest wording was straightforward: when you see "malformed tunnel record framing", look in `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/neighbour.rs`. That route came from an overlap between the issue name and the call name, not from a conclusion based on the full call chain. It was once enough to get investigators into the daemon-related directories, which is why it has been retained to this day; but treating it as implementation ownership will lead subsequent checks astray.

The file itself belongs to an existing Rust module and is suitable for code reading and checking historical behavior. The top of the entry file shows:

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::io;
use std::net::IpAddr;
use futures_util::TryStreamExt;
```

Based on this, the old record once stated that "the framing problem is in stream traversal". That judgment was too broad and did not receive enough support during the later review. `TryStreamExt` only shows that this code is adjacent to an asynchronous stream that may fail on individual items or end; `io`, `IpAddr`, and `HashMap` each point to different areas to inspect. They do not automatically combine into a path in which "partial frames are consumed by the neighbour module".

The migration sequence below retains the old entry point while moving the points that actually need confirmation back to the caller directory. It is suitable for cases that still come in through historical links but require renewed verification of malformed tunnel record framing.

## Start with the Old Label, Not a Conclusion

First, use the old label to find the relevant context. The old label serves two purposes: it can lead people to the relevant daemon code area, and it can remind them that this is a legacy issue left over from a compatibility check. Do not write "located in neighbour.rs" at this stage. The old entry point should only be recorded as: the issue name and call name once pointed here.

Next, obtain the directory structure provided by the caller and follow the actual direction of calls. At each stopping point, record just three small details: what object the previous layer handed over, whether object boundaries are still recognizable at this layer, and whether progress stopped because of termination, an error, or a lack of further directory relationships to inspect. There is no need to assume the internal layout of a tunnel record here; the frozen material provides no field formats, length rules, or parsing functions, so a set of framing rules cannot be invented from the names.

The relationship between the old and new paths is as follows:

```text
Old record
Issue name / Call name
        |
        v
neighbour.rs

Recheck
Caller directory -> Actual call site -> Handoff object -> Stop location
                                      |
                                      +-> neighbour state
                                      |
                                      +-> Adjacency to reading or conversion
                                      |
                                      +-> No concrete path yet
```

This diagram is not a call graph. It only constrains how the record is written: the old entry can continue to direct readers to `neighbour.rs`, but the actual processing point must be determined by where this traversal stops.

## Branches After Reaching neighbour.rs

After entering `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/neighbour.rs`, do not immediately search for "bad records". First ask whether the current operation is part of netlink neighbour state. If it is, record the name of the neighbour-state object and the object handed off by the previous layer, then return to the caller to confirm whether the two really connect. DOC-21 retain only the history of rolled-back trial runs and have no current acceptance tasks; old trial results are not carried over here, and cached state is not treated as a synonym for framing.

If the current code is only waiting for the next item or collecting a particular batch of state, shift the focus to how the stream terminates. `TryStreamExt` is worth examining in this scenario, but write the records separately:

- If an error is returned, retain the context related to `io` so that the generic label "bad frame" is not all that remains later;
- On normal termination, confirm whether a complete upstream object has already been obtained, rather than recording termination itself as truncation;
- When an object is converted to an address form, distinguish `IpAddr` handling from input record boundaries;
- If the container already holds state, confirm whether `HashMap` stores neighbour information or objects that the caller has already extracted.

Here, "confirm" is a requirement for writing notes about the observed situation, not an assertion that these conditions have each occurred. The biggest gap in the old version was that it described possible branches as causes that had already occurred. The new version retains only directions that can be rechecked using the file header and the caller directory.

## Correction After a Review

The additional review carried out later did not narrow malformed tunnel record framing down to a single module. The strong claim in the old entry should be withdrawn: **Do not conclude that malformed tunnel record framing is implemented or fixed by that file solely because `neighbour.rs` appears next to the issue name or call name.**

This correction does not mean that the old entry point is invalid. The old entry point can still serve two purposes: investigating why the earlier investigation ended up on the neighbour-state side, and checking whether streaming reads, address objects, and state containers were present at the same time. It no longer means that "finding the file is enough to complete the migration".

The task left by VPN-214 is to reproduce the behavior from the caller's directory structure and confirm the actual path at which traversal stops. The card changed assignees after an on-call schedule adjustment, and subsequent public notes still listed IPsec, netlink state, and malformed tunnel record framing together as one unconfirmed item. This shows that the investigation at the time covered more than just a section of framing; therefore, this page does not interpret IPsec state as direct evidence of tunnel records or use it to rewrite the module's responsibilities.

## What an Actual Migration Record Should Look Like

The new entry does not need to restate all the background at length. A useful addendum can be as simple as the following:

> The caller hands off an object in a directory; on proceeding to the next layer, traversal stops because of an error, termination, or a gap in the directory structure. If the next layer is `neighbour.rs`, separately note whether it was handling neighbour state or waiting for a stream item at the time. Do not label it as a framing processing point before seeing object boundaries.

Compared with the early approach of "assigning ownership as soon as a file is seen", this style preserves one more stopping point but creates one fewer false conclusion. It also allows different situations to produce different results: some return to neighbour state, some continue tracing reads or conversions, and some can only stop at the caller directory. All three outcomes can be included in the migration record; they must not be forcibly merged just to keep navigation tidy.

## How to Restore Old Links

If the new round of traversal only retraces the old navigation, or cannot establish object relationships more specific than "the call name points to neighbour.rs", restore the original link rather than replacing it with a guessed subpath. When restoring it, keep a one-line explanation: this entry point is for historical location guidance, and the specific processing point remains unconfirmed. This keeps the old page from breaking and prevents new misattributions from being written into the directory.

If traversal reaches a definite call site, first note the handoff object and the reason it stopped next to that site, then add them to this page. Do not delete the old entry point; instead, append a note saying "rechecked via the caller path". Readers can still enter through the original links and can also see why they should no longer read only `neighbour.rs`.

If the observed situation shows address conversion or neighbour-cache state, with no identifiable record boundaries, do not change the title or repackage an address issue as malformed framing. Just leave that observation under the corresponding object; this page retains only the fact that it intersected with the old path. DOC-21 are only for tracing rolled-back trial runs; VPN-217 govern the current neighbour-state conventions.

## Questions Still Left on This Page

- The actual path at which the caller-directory traversal stopped has not yet been recorded on this page.
- There is still only historical navigation to explain why the old call name consistently directs investigations to neighbour.rs, with no finer-grained record of the relationship.
- IPsec and netlink state were mentioned together at the time; whether they shared the same upstream input remains unconfirmed.
- When a stream ends early, whether enough objects are already available in the observed situation to judge that a record is complete still needs to be documented based on the actual call site.

Thus, this page remains usable but outdated migration material: it preserves the old entry point, a withdrawn judgment, and the sequence for restarting traversal. Future additions should focus on the actual stopping point, rather than once again interpreting the dependencies in the file header as a complete framing implementation.

This shows that the daemon, upstream, fallback, and disable-system rules are distinguished by name. It does not directly show which layer generates the probe or establish that the object handed off is already a complete forward-policy record.

There were two framings at the time: treating the handoff as a function call, or as a routing result produced by the daemon. The latter was adopted initially so failure symptoms and routing changes could be kept in one place. That decision was not on firm ground, because `routing.rs` also declared `IpOperation`, `IpFamily`, and `RouteType`; the file's scope was broader than the probe itself.

### Changes from the First Review

Later notes for VPN-223 broke the issue down into one successful call and one failed call. For the successful path, we need to know how the probe generation input is passed on for subsequent processing; for the failure path, the output observed at failure must be retained, not just a note saying "not generated". The material retained at the time was still insufficient to identify one particular function as the sole entry point, so the routing constants are not treated as handoff API here.

The review also shifted the notion of a "result" slightly away from the routing table itself. A forward-policy dump fragment can be used to observe the handoff, but a fragment is only a form of input, not automatically a complete record. If it is split during transfer, later readers must be able to distinguish "no target" from "the target has not yet appeared in this fragment". This is a requirement for the record format, not an inference about this file's implementation.

### Approaches Considered

At one point, the idea was to record only the declaration of `routing.rs` and attribute the probe to the caller. That would have been the shortest version, but it would have left no place for the failed call; recording only a successful call would also make the handoff look like a stable, one-way transfer. Another option was to list all routing priorities in a protocol table. It would be easy to look things up, but it would also make the ordering of rules unrelated to the probe part of the decision.

We are keeping the middle-ground approach: `routing.rs` as the starting point for verification, successful/failed calls as the two kinds of observed samples, and a fragment only as a handoff artifact that still needs to be checked. The file-header dependencies are also retained here to avoid turning navigation into a conclusion: `HashSet`, `io`, `IpAddr`, `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr`, and `Ipv4Inet` all appear in the file header, but they cannot on their own establish the direction of probe generation calls.

### Unresolved Points

The failed call's return boundary is still unknown, and there is not enough material to confirm whether the same object is shared before and after generation. The next record must at least capture the successful call's input/output and the failed call's input/output side by side; pasting priority constants alone cannot replace those two sets of results.

The navigation to VPN-223 is retained here. It leads to the investigation into probe generation inputs and environmental effects, but it does not turn the partial notes on that card into a full implementation description.

# Probe Generation Handoff Decision

The probe generation handoff was initially documented next to routing.rs because the daemon boundary could be identified during investigation from the routing priorities and type declarations. The four constants in the file occupy different ranges in sequence:

```rust
const RULE_PRIORITY_DAEMON_BASE: u32 = 20600;
const RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_BASE: u32 = 20700;
const RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_FALLBACK_BASE: u32 = 20800;
const RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_DISABLE_SYSTEM_BASE: u32 = 20900;
```

Early records treated these constants as the framework of the handoff. They do separate the priority ranges for daemon, upstream, fallback, and disable-system, but there is no probe generation call here, nor are there field definitions for a handoff object. This old assessment remains in the document because it explains why the first investigation started with this file; it can no longer serve as the current decision.

The same location in the file also contains `IpOperation`, `IpFamily`, and `RouteType`. Therefore, `routing.rs` is better suited as a local verification entry point than as something directly designated the probe producer. The dependencies at the top of the file can also only help identify local operations:

```rust
use std::collections::HashSet;
use std::io;
use std::net::{IpAddr, Ipv4Addr, Ipv6Addr};
use cidr::Ipv4Inet;
```

These declarations show that the file works with collections, IO, addresses, and IPv4 subnet types; they do not combine generation, transfer, and consumption into a single interface.

## Scope Left by the Early Decision

Three ways of describing the handoff were compared at the time.

The first described the handoff as a function call. The benefit was that readers could continue following the call site, and there was also a place to look for failure returns; the problem was that the call marking the generation boundary had not yet been confirmed, so naming it prematurely would turn a local guess into an interface fact.

The second described the handoff as a routing result. The four priority constants appeared to support this account, and readers could understand the ordering relationship between daemon and upstream. However, routing results are subsequently visible state and cannot replace the inputs and outputs at the time of probe generation; a failed call might not even have any rules that could be installed, so inferring generation backward from the results would miss the evidence from the call.

The third treated a forward-policy dump as the sole handoff format. It could preserve inputs and outputs as comparable fragments and was particularly useful for recording environmental effects, but fragments still have boundaries. The absence of a target in one fragment might mean the target really does not exist, or it might mean the target is in another fragment. Describing it as a complete dump would lead to misinterpretations about compatibility.

The early decision adopted the second option, but was later revised to preserve the distinction among the three kinds of objects: calls are a verification path, routing results are observations, and a forward-policy dump fragment is evidence of the transfer. This change does not delete the old material; it limits the conclusions that each kind of material can support.

## Handoff Records Established After Review

Later records in VPN-223 require the visible results of one successful call and one failed call to be preserved separately. Here, "success" does not generally mean that the daemon is operating normally; it means that the call actually produced output that could be observed further. "Failure" is not recorded as a single error category either; at a minimum, the inputs and outputs seen at the time of failure must be preserved. This makes it possible to determine whether the handoff occurred before discussing whether the routing state changed.

This page uses the following recording sequence: first confirm the verification entry point from the local declarations in `routing.rs`, then preserve call samples, and finally flag fragment completeness issues separately. With this change in sequence, priorities no longer serve as proof of the interface.

```text
routing.rs declarations
        -> probe call input
        -> handoff output or failure output
        -> forward-policy dump fragment
        -> route observation
```

This diagram shows only the connections between the verification steps on this page, not the complete end-to-end call chain in the source code. It also does not mean that every failed call reaches route observation; a failure may stop at an earlier handoff boundary.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Verification entry point" as Locate
    state "Call sample" as Call
    state "Handoff output" as Output
    state "Failure output" as Failure
    state "Fragment check" as Fragment
    state "Route observation" as Route
    [*] --> Locate
    Locate --> Call
    Call --> Output: success
    Call --> Failure: failure
    Output --> Fragment
    Fragment --> Route
    Failure --> [*]
```

### Successful Calls

Successful samples need to preserve three kinds of information: what input was seen before generation, what output remained after the handoff, and how the output was observed by the next stage. The input and output should come from the same call and cannot be supplemented afterward with the result of another successful call. If only the routing priority constants remain, they can at most explain the tiers of rule naming; they cannot reconstruct this handoff.

This is why the document was later changed from a "routing history" to a "handoff history". The issue with probe generation is not listing more rule names, but determining whether the generated result left the current boundary and what was retained when it did.

### Failed Calls

Failure samples must be kept separate from successful samples. On failure, empty output must not be interpreted as "no probe", nor must unchanged routing be interpreted as generation not having occurred. First, it is necessary to determine whether the failure occurred during input parsing, at the call return, or during subsequent observation; the currently frozen material does not provide a specific exception, so no error code or function name is filled in here.

The earlier claim that "failure means no generation" is no longer valid. It conflates visible results with internal actions and cannot explain why a forward-policy dump fragment was preserved. The current record only decides to preserve failure inputs/outputs and makes no additional attribution about the failure boundary.

## Fragment Compatibility Issues

An intermediate review positioned the forward-policy dump fragment as a handoff observation. The value of a fragment is that it allows inputs and outputs to be compared side by side as they are; its limitations are equally clear: chunk order, chunk boundaries, and whether target records span chunks all affect the reader's judgment about "no target".

Therefore, "this fragment contains no record" can only be recorded as a local observation. Whether the target truly does not exist can only be discussed after seeing the complete dump. The current material provides neither a complete dump nor a fixed chunk size or reassembly interface, so these details cannot be filled in.

This was also a rejected alternative: treating each fragment as an independent result and taking the failure branch directly whenever an empty fragment is encountered. This approach is simple to implement, but it turns transport boundaries into business semantics; once a target record spans fragments, a successful call may be incorrectly recorded as a failure. Preserving the original fragment boundaries is safer than joining them into a seemingly complete result.

## Relationship to Adjacent Decisions

DOC-23 document the interface review for fallback-route selection / Android local route table. It shares the route observation side with this page, but that does not mean it takes responsibility for probe generation inputs or failure attribution. This page allows routing changes to be treated as observations only after the handoff has left output; upstream selection and the generation boundary on this page remain documented separately.

This boundary corrects the earlier practice of writing them together: seeing `RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_BASE` and `RULE_PRIORITY_UPSTREAM_FALLBACK_BASE` next to each other previously made it easy to treat upstream selection as the next decision in the probe handoff. Adjacency does not mean they are the same interface. For the current revision, what can be confirmed is the constant declarations and their named ranges; callers cannot be inferred from line numbers.

## Counterexamples and Evidence Recording

Three kinds of records will mislead subsequent verification.

* Paste only the four priority constants, then write "the probe has been handed off to upstream". This presents a naming relationship as the result of an action.
* Preserve only successful output and delete failure output. This hides the inputs under which the handoff stopped.
* Treat a forward-policy dump fragment as a complete dump. This incorrectly treats targets spanning fragments as absent.

The revised evidence records should preserve the pairing without forcing unknown fields to be filled in:

```text
Successful call
input: <original input from the same call>
output: <visible output from the same call>
Observation: <routing or policy changes observed afterward>

Failed call
input: <original input from the failed call>
output: <output or error context actually left at the time of failure>
Observation: No confirmable subsequent result was produced
```

The text in angle brackets does not represent existing samples and cannot be filled in by this page. It only marks the paired positions that should be preserved when pasting in evidence later; the current input provides no specific payload, exception text, or call symbols, so no set of "real" outputs is fabricated.

## Decisions Currently Retained

1. `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/routing.rs` serves only as a local verification entry point for the probe generation handoff; the filename is not treated as proof of generator ownership.
2. Inputs and outputs must be preserved separately for successful calls and failed calls; routing constants cannot replace these two sets of evidence.
3. A forward-policy dump fragment can be used as handoff observation material, but the absence of a target from a fragment does not directly establish that the target is absent from the complete dump.
4. route observation is recorded after the handoff output. It describes visible results and does not work backward to determine the generation action.

The decisions here address documentation and verification boundaries, rather than filling in implementation details in the source code that have not yet been frozen. What remains unconfirmed is: the exact boundary of the failure return, the specific structure of the generated result, where fragment reassembly occurs, and which subsequent component consumes successful output. When new evidence becomes available, prioritize adding a pair of inputs/outputs from the same call; do not just append more priority constants.

VPN-223 remain the navigation entry point for investigating probe generation inputs and environmental effects. Related records can help locate successful and failed samples, but cannot replace this page's distinction between the two kinds of samples.

# Fallback Route Interface Proposal

The first note treated "the words fallback and route appear in the file" as a clue to where the implementation belonged. After review, that assessment needs to be narrowed: `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/shared/model.rs` is a useful starting point for tracing back, but it only shows that the model declarations involve both address and protocol objects. It does not show that this file has sole ownership of selection. The `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr`, `Ipv6Cidr`, `Ipv6Inet`, and `MasqueradeMode` in the file header are still worth keeping; the call edges are not expanded in the material on this page.

### Two approaches considered in review

**Keep it in the model layer.** The model object takes the destination address and available routes, and returns the configured fallback network when no primary route matches. This gives the selection rules a single entry point, so callers don't have to interpret "no match" individually. The trade-off is that the timing of Android local route table reads must be fixed; if the table is updated elsewhere, the model layer may only have a stale view.

**Leave it to the caller.** The model layer only stores route data, and the caller that owns the Android local route table decides between primary and fallback. This puts the decision closer to the data source, but every caller has to understand the same no-match semantics, so more interface examples and compatibility handling will be needed later.

This review did not obtain results from actual calls, so neither approach can be recorded as a decision. Retain "centralize selection in the model layer" as the working assumption for now, and make the caller version, entry point, and state of the table passed in required checks. If the caller has already selected a fallback itself, the model-layer approach would repeat selection; if it only accepts a primary match, changing the interface would cost more than just swapping out a return value.

The withdrawal conditions are noted here: do not move selection logic without evidence from an actual caller; if a dependency on the old return shape is found, maintain compatibility first, then discuss migration separately. Which object owns the final selection decision is still unresolved.

# Fallback Routing Interface Proposal

This page started with `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/shared/model.rs`. The file header imports `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6Addr`, `Ipv6Cidr`, `Ipv6Inet` and `MasqueradeMode`, so the early notes naturally treated it as "the place where route selection happens." That assessment was later narrowed: the path helps locate the model declarations, but does not show how callers obtain the Android local route table or prove that selection necessarily happens in this file.

The first design review recorded both directions. Keeping selection in the model layer gives a more centralized interface: callers only need to supply the destination address and the current routing data. But table refresh timing must be stable, or the model layer will make decisions using a stale table. Delegating selection to the caller puts it closer to the owner of the Android local route table, but different callers Fang Ke can each handle primary misses independently, spreading out the interface semantics. Someone once took "the model layer mentions fallback" to mean the first approach was already implemented. That is an old assessment, retained here for reference and no longer treated as an implementation conclusion.

Follow-up review broke the issue down into several practical boundaries. Checking whether the returned object is empty is not enough; we also need to check whether the destination address matches a primary route, whether the fallback network is a configured value or one assembled ad hoc by the caller, and whether the caller treats a miss as an error. If route table refresh and selection happen in different layers, the review also needs to document when the table was observed; otherwise, the same destination address may see different candidates between two checks. The available material includes neither real call examples nor test output, so no function names, commands or results are filled in here.

The latest note corrected the earlier claim that a primary miss is a failure. The interface semantics to retain are:

> When no primary route matches, upstream selection returns the configured fallback network, including Some(9) for fallback network 9.

This sentence changes how the selection result is interpreted; it does not confirm ownership of `model.rs`. The fallback is a configured network, not a generic substitute for an empty value. Callers still need to state which observation of the Android local route table supplied the routing data they pass to the selection logic. Centralized selection in the model layer can remain a design candidate, but this is still a limited proposal within the interface review, not the current authoritative guidance.

Migration costs also need to be assessed against the actual structure of each caller. If a caller is found to have already performed selection, revert the change that repeats selection to avoid applying fallback to the same destination again. If an old caller only accepts primary matches, preserve the old return shape first, then add a compatibility layer before migrating; do not change both the table source and the return semantics in a single consolidation. If the only change is the addition of fields to model declarations, with no changes to call edges, that cannot be taken as evidence that selection logic has migrated.

Open decisions:

- Which caller actually holds the Android local route table;
- The order of route table refresh and upstream selection;
- Whether the compatibility layer needs to cover old callers, rather than only changing model declarations;
- Whether reading the fallback network configuration and the routing data in use belong to the same lifecycle.

Until verification results are available, withdrawal criteria take precedence over migration steps: without call edges and example results, do not move selection logic; if a dependency on the old return shape is found, do not force a replacement in the name of a "centralized interface." Related background can be cross-checked via DOC-24, but it is not the basis for this page's fallback selection conclusion.

This review covers only primary and fallback route precedence. After seeing a primary result in the legacy call, it's easy to treat this step as if upstream selection were already complete; during migration, record "whether the destination address matches primary" separately from "the fallback that can still be used when it doesn't match."

versions.body:
# Primary/Standby Route Priority Compatibility Flow

This page initially left only one reminder: do not treat a single check of primary as the entire upstream selection. During later review, it became clear that the genuinely difficult part was not adding fallback, but that old call sites encoded "no primary match" as several different intermediate states. Some call sites would continue to retrieve the configured fallback, while others stopped early in their own branches. On the surface, both lacked a primary result, but their post-migration behavior should not be conflated.

This round still starts from the call relationships around the shared model. `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/src/shared/model.rs` retains shared type references related to addresses and the IPv6 subnet: `Ipv4Addr`, `Ipv6`, `Ipv6Cidr`, and `Ipv6Inet`, as well as `MasqueradeMode` in the daemon protocol. This is not a complete inventory of the routing strategy implementation, but records involving target addresses, subnet interpretation, and upstream network selection during migration should all be cross-checked outward from here. First confirm which type of address the call site obtains, then confirm which downstream object it hands the selection result to; looking only at primary or fallback in variable names is insufficient to determine priority.

## Retaining the Old Record

The draft's "continue checking fallback after a primary miss" was not removed, but at the time it did not distinguish between two old patterns.

The first old pattern is that, after the primary query returned an empty result, the call site still proceeded through the same selection flow, but the original record did not capture the source or return value of fallback. These call sites can be organized according to the current order, with the focus on completing the review record.

The second old pattern converted the empty primary result into its own failure branch. It might cut off subsequent selection, or it might expose only "no available network" to the caller. These call sites cannot be migrated by replacing the condition alone; first confirm whether they actually enforce the business constraint that fallback is not allowed. If they do not, remove the early exit and return them to the shared selection order. If they do, retain the reason next to the call site instead of pretending it is equivalent to the normal path.

The early records did not explain this distinction; it was only added as a migration prerequisite in a later note. The old paragraph is retained because it can still explain why some call sites are completed by changing only one place, while others require checking the caller's own exit branch.

## Three Items to Collect Before Migration

Each candidate call site only needs to retain the local information relevant to this change:

- the input target address, and whether the address is derived before entering selection or inside the call site;
- whether the primary query result has already been converted into a Boolean, an exception branch, or some other local state;
- where the fallback network enters from configuration, and whom the call site ultimately hands the selection result to.

These three items must be placed in the same review excerpt. Saving only the primary return value will not show whether the call site exits early; saving only the fallback configuration will not confirm whether it actually participates in selection. For the IPv6 address, also check whether the address is first classified into some `Ipv6Cidr`. There is no need to reread every type in the shared model; just confirm that the target address is not converted by another layer into a different comparison object before entering route selection.

Do not write primary and fallback as two unrelated switches. The former is the priority match, while the latter is the continued selection when primary cannot match the target address. The migrated call site should retain this order instead of reading fallback first and then using it to overwrite a primary that has already matched.

```text
Path that is easy to misread before migration
Target address -> primary query -> empty result -> call site exits early

Selection path after migration
Target address -> primary query -> match: use primary
                         \\-> no match: check configured fallback
```

The "early exit" in the diagram is not a standardized name for an old implementation, but a control-flow position that needs to be found during review. If the call site continues after a primary miss but fallback appears only in an error-handling branch, treat it as an early exit as well: first move fallback back into the normal no-match branch, then check whether the original error branch still has other responsibilities.

## Migrate by Call Site

1. First fix one target address as the review input. Do not use "default network available" as a substitute for checking the address; the priority difference in this change occurs precisely when primary has no match for that address.

2. Record the action that occurs immediately after the primary query. If the result is saved, trace it to the first point that decides whether to return; if it is used directly in a conditional, record the two exits of that condition. The goal here is to find where the miss is consumed, not to count how many queries there are in total.

3. Locate the configuration entry for the fallback network. It may already be visible at the call site, or it may be passed in by a higher layer. During migration, do not copy the configuration into a local temporary variable to bypass the original entry; that would turn the priority issue into a configuration synchronization issue in two places.

4. Connect fallback selection in the normal branch where primary misses. The current compatibility criterion is: when no primary route matches the target address, upstream network selection returns the configured fallback network. In the review sample, this return value is recorded as `Some(9)`; it means that selection has fallen back to the configured fallback, not that it is an alias for a primary match.

5. Preserve the original selection when primary matches; do not use fallback to overwrite the result. Migration is not about changing every call site to favor fallback, but about making fallback handle only addresses that primary does not match.

6. For call sites that originally exited early, check once more whether the upper layer depends on that exit state. If the upper layer merely treats it as "no primary," it can be changed to receive the fallback selection result; if the upper layer genuinely needs to distinguish between no match and being forbidden to continue selection, retain that boundary and do not label it a compatibility path.

Handle only one call site per change. When multiple call sites share the same address-preparation logic, they may share address samples, but do not skip their individual exit branches just because the samples are the same. In actual migrations, errors usually occur in local checks after the shared query, not in the shared model types themselves.

## How to Record Sample Review

A sample was attached before the maintenance window. Its value is that it places the target address, the primary miss, and the fallback return in the same record, rather than proving that every caller has been migrated. The review should show at least that:

- the input address did not match primary;
- the call site did not return at that empty result;
- fallback came from the existing configuration entry;
- the final selection matched the configured fallback.

If the sample shows only the final network number, still add the context showing whether the primary query missed; otherwise, `Some(9)` may be misread as the primary result. If the sample shows only that primary was empty, that is also insufficient to assert that fallback took effect, because the call site may have stopped afterward. Both pieces of information must be stored next to each other.

For an address that matches primary, there is no need to reconstruct a complete fallback sample in the same batch. It is enough to verify that this branch does not read fallback and overwrite the existing selection. This keeps the migration review focused on the boundary that actually changed instead of revalidating the original match path.

## Handling After the Maintenance Window

After the sample was attached, one review from the original plan was not completed within the window, and the card was subsequently suspended. The reason for suspension was that the maintenance window closed; it does not mean that fallback behavior was rejected, nor that all candidate call sites were confirmed. A later public note still indicated that one point in primary and fallback route precedence remained unconfirmed; therefore, this page does not treat the sample as a completion marker.

When resuming the work, continue from the unfinished check at VPN-210. First find one caller that is still using this priority, and record the actual version, the location where it enters selection, and the current result. After selecting a caller, do not batch-edit adjacent paths first; first confirm whether it belongs to one of the two old patterns, "continue selection" or "exit early." If neither pattern fits, keep the call site separately in the verification record instead of forcing it into a category just to apply the migration steps.

DOC-26 records another set of daemon closeout checks involving relay timeout shutdown classification and kernel release parser boundary. They can serve as navigation items for the same maintenance batch, but do not use their conclusions to infer that route priority is complete; route selection is still determined by the address, the primary result, and the fallback configuration on this page.

## Restoring the Old Path

If a migrated call site produces an upper-layer state that differs from the old path when primary misses, first restore its original exit position instead of immediately changing the shared model or fallback configuration. During restoration, retain three pieces of context: the target address, the raw result of the primary query, and where the call site stopped. This allows later review to determine whether the problem came from the newly connected fallback branch or whether the old caller simply did not accept continued selection.

Do not manufacture the old behavior by deleting the fallback configuration. The configuration may still be used by other migrated call sites; deleting it would turn one call site's fallback into a global behavior change. The correct restoration scope is the branch belonging to that call site: undo its change from entering fallback after a primary miss, restore the original return or error exit, and list the call site again among the items pending review.

If the primary-match path changes, first revert the condition rewrite at that call site as well. A primary match should not become fallback because of this migration; if that happens, the condition is in the wrong place or the result-overwrite order is wrong. After restoration, the address sample can be retained for another review in the next window; there is no need to rebuild the entire migration batch.

## What Is Not Yet Closed Out

What remains unconfirmed is what state the one caller still using this priority actually interprets a primary miss as. # Quality Signal Dashboard Dual-State Postmortem

This anomaly began with a failing sample related to test. The entry point showed two states at closely spaced check times, with the object name on the page unchanged but the current revision inconsistent. The first person to see it treated it as ordinary entry-point lag; the original record, the recovery page, and the unconfirmed cause were subsequently preserved side by side, so the earlier assessment did not automatically become a conclusion when the page turned green again.

The initial impact was on regression tiering, not on every test. The Quality Signal Dashboard originally used failing samples to distinguish reproducible regressions from unstable signals. When the same object kept alternating between two states, this sample could not go straight into the stable tier. Only automatic classification for this one sample was disabled during the response, and the other samples were not also declared invalid. The Quality Signal Dashboard still has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; for the exit window, see [DOC-40](DOC-40).

## Evidence recorded over time

| Time | What was observed at the time | Action taken |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `LICENSE-Quality Signal Dashboard-The same object shows two states` first deviated from the previously observed state | Preserved the entry-point observations, original input, and original record |
| T+07 | `transparent proxy` was still normal | Initially narrowed the impact to this failing sample and its classification |
| T+18 | The focus of comparison shifted to `IPv6 extension header` | Recorded it as a working hypothesis, without closing the anomaly |
| T+31 | The recovery page showed that the user path had recovered | Recorded the recovery time separately, without marking it as root-cause confirmation |

The simple diagram recorded at the time showed only this relationship, without expanding it into a complete call graph:

```text
test failure sample
      |
      v
Quality Signal Dashboard entry point -- two states --> original record / recovery page
      |
      +-- the current revision differed at the two observation times
```

What the entry point initially showed was a state conflict, not a confirmed failure mechanism. The old record preserved the first packet quote observed, while the recovery page preserved the result after the postcondition check passed again. Readers looking only at the recovery page would assume that the earlier failure evidence was no longer valid; readers looking only at the original record would miss the fact that the user path had recovered. Neither set of evidence superseded the other.

## Why the assessment at the time did not hold up

The current revision shown at the original entry point was the reason this record was repeatedly revisited later. The values observed at the two times differed, but the page did not indicate between which checks the change had occurred. The first version attributed the difference to display updates lagging behind the signal. That explanation could describe "what looked like two states", but it did not explain whether the states came from the same object or the order of the two values.

The first version also presented "slow entry-point updates" too directly, making it read as though the cause had already been established. In fact, all that was available at the time was one packet quote mismatch, two entry-point observations, and one page of recovery results. No record proved that entry-point updates were the only change, and no record proved that the two states were caused by object replacement. Later handoffs mentioned "two objects", but that was only a working classification for organizing the tiering table, and object boundaries cannot be inferred from the available evidence.

At T+07, the normal result from `transparent proxy` was the direct basis for narrowing the scope of impact. It showed that this user path had not failed at the same time as the dashboard entry point, so broader recovery actions were not initiated. It could not prove that the entry point had only a display issue, nor could it rule out another change related to state reads. The old handoff made a stronger claim about "the proxy being normal", and that earlier account remains in the record because it explains why the response was not expanded at the time.

At T+18, `IPv6 extension header` was also only a lead for comparison. The reviewer saw that the comparison point was there and noted it alongside the anomaly, trying to explain the packet quote mismatch. No result showing "the two states merged after changing this location" was recorded, nor was there a continuous record linking it to the change in the current revision. The old draft placed this observation very early, making it easy to mistake a comparison lead for the root cause; this version retains it as a source of the mistaken assessment at the time.

## Stopping retries and assessing recovery

The failing sample was not retried further. This was not because retries had been proven to corrupt data, but because a later state would become mixed into the initial evidence, making it impossible to tell which state belonged to the first deviation when comparing the entry point, the original record, and the recovery page. The on-duty staff therefore preserved the input and entry-point version from the first failure, and stopped including this sample in the stable regression tier for the time being.

The only recovery result available later was a passing postcondition check. It was appropriate for marking "user path recovered", not for marking "root cause confirmed". The old version described the recovery actions and diagnostic completion in the same paragraph, making it easy for readers to interpret recovery as meaning that the anomaly had been explained. The second version separated the two times, but did not fill in a causal chain to compensate for the missing evidence: why the forward policy dump changed was still unknown, and there was also no conclusion on whether it shared an origin with the two states.

The green result after recovery did not supersede what happened in the initial failure window. If only the recovery page were retained, later readers would not see the first packet quote or the inconsistent current revision at the two times; if only the original record were retained, they would miss the fact that the path had recovered. Both sets of evidence were placed under the same incident entry point so that the state conflict and recovery result could be read in sequence, not so that one would be treated as a revision of the other.

## Scope of impact

This response addressed attribution for a single failing sample, not a decision to disable the entire Quality Signal Dashboard. The sample was no longer used as a stable signal during the window, to prevent inconsistent states from continuing to enter regression tiering. No evidence indicated that the normal result from `transparent proxy` should be deleted, and no evidence indicated that all samples related to IPv6 should be withdrawn along with this sample.

The Quality Signal Dashboard retains the failing samples, regression tiering, and unstable-signal attribution produced around test. It has its own independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; behavior in adjacent projects was not automatically included in this incident because of this entry-point anomaly. The old version described the scope more broadly, as though a state difference at one entry point could explain all related tests. That account is retained as the historical position, but the current evidence supports only the localized impact described above.

## Ways of organizing the records that were not adopted

Someone suggested retaining only the recovery page, because the entry point could continue to be used after recovery. This approach was not adopted. The recovery page could show only the results after T+31, and could not replace the input, packet quote, and original record from T+00. Another suggestion was to split the two states directly into two independent objects and place each in the tiering table. That would make the table tidier, but it presupposed that object identity had changed, and the available evidence did not support that premise.

An even quicker way to write it up would have been to record `IPv6 extension header` directly as the cause, then use the normal result from `transparent proxy` as an exclusion criterion. The evidence at the time did not include enough change results to support that attribution, and the proxy being normal covered only one comparison path. These two observations therefore remained recorded at their respective times, rather than being assembled into an explanation that became complete only in hindsight.

## The unfilled window

The gap is concentrated between the two states. What needs to be confirmed is: whether there are raw records of the order in which the current revision changed; whether the original record and the recovery page always pointed to the same object; and whether the comparison at T+18 corresponded to the state change, rather than merely occurring at the same time. The current evidence does not answer these questions.

When encountering the same kind of entry point again, first preserve the input, observed states, and entry-point version from that occurrence, then determine whether the failing sample should remain excluded from the stable tier. The reading order should still start with the original record and then move to the recovery page, and the recovered state must not replace the first deviation. If only the recovery result can be found, with no evidence of the first deviation, it can only be recorded as impossible to determine, and "slow entry-point updates" cannot be reused as a new characterization.

This postmortem can continue to help distinguish "the user path has recovered" from "the source of the states has been explained", but its statements about entry-point lag, proxy impact, and extension headers all carry the temporal context of the time. The change in the forward policy dump, the object relationship underlying the two states, and the missing intervening window remain unconfirmed.

# Quality Signal Console Window Exit Checklist

Two requirements from the old version still stand: the original entry point must be retained, and a single "success" log entry cannot replace the exit action. The old version also treated `transparent proxy` as a blanket signal not to clear the state. That rule later proved insufficient, but was not removed; it reflected the situation at the time, when it was not possible to tell whether the proxy was still occupying the window.

Before starting this run, use `docs/adj-license/release/license-quality-signal-exit-window-checklist.md` to locate the original record. If a replay is needed, use the original input from "license-quality-signal Window Exit Checklist"—the license-quality-signal input—not a newly assembled similar input. The original input, the current entry point, and the original current revision are three different things: an entry point that opens does not mean the input is still there; having the input does not mean a result was recorded for the current revision.

## Checks before entering the window

- [ ] Starting at the time of recovery, look only for the first record for the current revision. If that first record is missing, do not use later summaries to fill in the assessment.
- [ ] Save the input for this run and the first result observed. If the input changes during the operation, record the result after the change in a new paragraph; do not overwrite the first result.
- [ ] Check the current entry point and the original current revision. If both are missing, leave the status as unknown; do not record it as zero results.
- [ ] Record the expiration time of each temporary permission, proxy, and environment. They are not part of the release status, but continuing to use them after they expire will prevent the exit process from being closed out.

This section carries over the sequence of work from the old checklist. A cleaned-up green result had previously been placed next to the original record, but was later found not to represent the state on entry to the window. That cleaned-up result may still be kept, as long as it is not treated as the first result.

## Where the old rule applies

When `transparent proxy` appears, first check which input instance and which period of temporary access it corresponds to. Continue closing the window only if it can be matched to an input that has already completed and the queue is no longer accepting work. If the mapping is unclear, preserve the state and stop further teardown. The old version's "do not clear the state" applies only to the latter case.

`desired routing mutation` is still the name of a stopping point, not a completion marker. If it has not been seen, you cannot infer that the exit failed, nor can you proceed to remove all remaining temporary resources. The record should include the last result seen at that point, the objects not yet removed, and the handoff entry point. If it appears only in a later step, record it under that step; do not backfill it as having already existed when the window opened.

- [ ] Confirm that the queue is no longer accepting new work after `shutdown boundary`.
- [ ] If work is still coming in, stop closing the window and retain the original input and the last result; do not clear the state just for the handoff.
- [ ] If no work is coming in, then revoke the temporary permissions and remove the bypasses. Before doing so, confirm that the result has been saved in the original record.

This check does not provide release sign-off on behalf of the responsible owner. It only indicates whether the exit actions on the adj-license side can continue, or where they should stop.

## What to record at handoff

The handoff record must now include the person handing off, the person taking over, and the confirmation time. Previous temporary assignees only replied about expiry actions; that does not mean anyone has reviewed every window. Remove retired groups from the new entry point. If action routing cannot find an actual person to take over, retain the current entry point; do not keep listing the old group name as an available destination.

VPNC-011 document the search for the actual person taking over based on LICENSE · Quality Signal Board's actions; this does not change the original owner's release sign-off. VPNC-007 require contacting the original owner before the exit action is due; if there is no reply, close out using the existing exit actions. Here, "close out" means stop initiating new operations and retain the records, not declare the release a success.

A handoff addendum was recorded in VPNC-002, and the old assignee was removed because they had only reviewed it once. This change corrected a misdirected entry point; it does not guarantee that every subsequent window already has someone to take over. If any handoff field is missing, the window can remain paused with the saved result; a project team name cannot substitute for confirmation from an individual.

## Exception for the public environment

Local results are for diagnosis only. When the exit actions need to be rechecked, test once more through the public entry point using the original license-quality-signal; this is a to-do in VPNC-006. Until it is completed, do not elevate the local result to a conclusion about the public environment. If no result was saved in the public environment, do not fabricate a replay just to fill in the checklist.

Before exiting, check the current entry point and the original current revision again. The zero-result capture described in VPNC-012 is meaningful only when both are present; if both are missing, still record the status as unknown. The original-input replay in VPNC-013 is used to check whether the input was swapped out, not to replace a first result that has already been lost.

The last part of the old procedure still stands: if you cannot make a determination about `transparent proxy` or `desired routing mutation` is missing, stop first. Unlike in version 2, after stopping you must put the objects not removed, the last result, and the handoff record back at the original entry point. This checklist still does not confirm whether the recovery action has been tried in the shared environment.

# Dependency Boundary Failure On-Call Page

This page follows only one replay of gradlew-supply-boundary. At the start, put the original input, the current revision, the page state, and the first output in the same record; the value ultimately displayed on the page is corroborating evidence only and cannot replace the order in which events occurred.

## Entering the scene

Open this project's entry point from `docs/adj-gradlew/runbooks/gradlew-dependency-boundary-audit-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. Confirm that the replay uses the original input; do not create a similar input. If the entry point has already been replaced, first record the page actually reached and the current revision, then stop; do not guess the path this run took from an old link.

When saving, do not restart, refresh permissions, or run another data set. A normal sample can be used to find differences, but change only one condition in each comparison. The record should start at the first difference, rather than being filled in after the run has finished.

## Find the first breakpoint

Review the replay in its original time order. When a difference is found, first check whether it is still within the dependency source, adoption scope, and exit responsibility managed by gradlew · Dependency Boundary Audit; if it has already crossed into a shared interface, hand over only the entry point and the on-site context, while the original project still retains the user-side record.

The replay of the original input for VPND-007 shows that the exit entry point failed at the third step. Record this breakpoint against the exit entry point; do not continue the replay just to obtain an ending. If the states before and after exit need to be compared, retain the route snapshot from before the change; residual state caused by the old exit action must not be deleted on the spot and then treated as the original state.

Stop immediately in the following cases:

- The original input cannot be found, or the input cannot be matched to the current replay object;
- The normal and failed samples changed more than one condition at the same time;
- The first difference occurred before the exit entry point, but the output for that step was not retained;
- After recovery, only a summary result is visible, and the first current revision record starting at the recovery point cannot be retrieved.

Write the handoff in the actual order: the entry point accessed, the original input used, the first difference, the stop action, the snapshot retained, and the guesses already ruled out.
