# On-Call Page for Failed Runs at the Dependency Boundary

First preserve a failed run in the order events occurred, without rushing to reach a conclusion of success or failure. This page covers replaying the original input for gradlew-supply-boundary: the on-call engineer enters through the entry point, finds the first difference, stops at the step that is no longer reliable, and preserves the state so the next person can continue assessing it.

The entry point is fixed at `docs/adj-gradlew/runbooks/gradlew-dependency-boundary-audit-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. It is a local page for gradlew · Dependency Boundary Audit, not an overview of the shared interface. On entry, first record three things: the object corresponding to the original input, the current revision, and the first visible output. The page's final value may remain in the record, but only as corroborating evidence; when the page timeline and the current revision do not match, reordering by the original timestamps takes priority.

## Do Not Fix the State Yet

When taking over a failed run, first preserve its untouched state. Do not restart immediately to rule out a transient issue, do not refresh permissions, do not recreate similar input, and do not start by deleting old exit actions. Doing so would mix the original breakpoint with the results of later manual changes.

You may use the most recent known-good sample as a reference, but only one condition may change in the comparison. Clearly record that condition before starting; if the two samples you have already differ in more than one of input, revision, or exit state, they can only show that the results differ and cannot be used to locate the first difference. At that point, stop comparing and return to the original input.

Also stop if the page cannot be opened, the entry point has been replaced, or the content you reach does not match the recorded project object. Just retain the page you actually reached, the current revision, and the known object. Do not reconstruct a speculative execution path from old links.

## Starting the Run Log

Start the run table with the first visible record, in the following order:

| Order | What the on-call engineer must retain | Conditions for continuing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry | Original input, current revision, initial output | Can confirm this is the same replay |
| Comparison | Most recent known-good sample and the only condition that changed | The two samples can be compared step by step |
| Divergence | First difference and the exit state at that time | The difference is still within this project's boundary |
| Stop | Last output before stopping, retained snapshots | Subsequent actions will not overwrite the state |
| Handoff | Actions taken, hypotheses ruled out, items to investigate | The next person can return to the same entry point |

The "first difference" is not the final red result, nor the final summary on the page. It is the earliest step in replay order that cannot be aligned with the known-good sample. If there is no output at the first difference, record "output missing", and do not skip it to choose a later section that looks more complete.

## When the Exit Entry Point Breaks at Step Three

This branch comes from replaying the original input. After the exit entry point breaks at step three, record the last confirmed state before step three, then write the breakpoint back to the exit entry point. End the replay here; do not continue running to the end just to obtain the final page.

Before stopping, preserve the pre-change route snapshot. VPND-008 notes that old exit actions leave residual routes, so when handling the state, do not delete the residual routes before checking the breakpoint. If cleanup is genuinely necessary, complete the record of the original state first, then record cleanup separately as a subsequent attempt; the page after cleanup must not overwrite the original output of this failed run.

On the exit branch, also check whether the object has been split into two states. VPND-015 requires retaining the two states of gradlew-supply-boundary in the order they occurred, and first determining whether they belong to the same object. If this cannot be determined, write "association unconfirmed" and keep the two records separately. Do not merge them just because the names are the same, and do not backfill the later state into the record before step three.

If a difference has already appeared before step three, the exit entry point should not be treated as the first failure. Record the exit entry point as a breakpoint encountered later, and keep the first difference in its original order. This prevents the next replay from mistakenly treating the exit issue as the entire cause.

## Data Retrieval After Recovery

After recovery, it is especially easy to mistake later summaries for the state at the time. Do not record it that way here. The approach in VPND-011 is to retrieve only the first current revision record starting from the recovery point, without looking at subsequent summaries for now. If that record cannot be retrieved, stop the post-recovery comparison and explicitly note "first record missing" in the handoff.

Successful recovery only means that the run did not remain stuck at that time, not that the exit entry point, original input, or dependency source has been proven normal. Do not write the green page after recovery back into the earlier failed steps. If there are two object states from before and after recovery, still retain them in the order they occurred; the recovery point is only the starting point for retrieving records, not a reason to clear the old states.

When the current revision does not match the page timeline, first look back at the original timestamps. The approach in VPND-004 is to reorder the current revision and the page by their original timestamps, using the page's final value only as corroborating evidence. If, after reordering, you still cannot determine which record belongs to this replay, leave that unknown and do not substitute the page's final value for the sequence.

## Differences Outside the Boundary

This page covers dependency sources, scope of adoption, and exit responsibilities associated with license. When the difference remains within this scope, continue following this page's rules for recording the original input, the single condition, and the first breakpoint. If the difference extends beyond this scope, do not assess the shared interface's implementation on this page.

When handing off to the shared interface, include only: this page's entry point, the object corresponding to the original input, the current revision, the first difference, and the retained snapshots. The original project continues to retain the user-side state, and the receiving party takes over only its own implementation portion. If no new records are returned after the handoff, stop this page at the handoff point and do not fill in the other party's subsequent results.

## Handoff Format

Do not write the handoff as "handled". Fill in at least the following lines:

- **Entry point used**: The path actually opened, and whether it is still the entry point listed on this page.
- **Original input**: Whether use of the original gradlew-supply-boundary input has been confirmed; if not, state what is missing.
- **Current revision**: The value seen on entry, and whether it matches the page timeline.
- **First difference**: The step, the output, and whether it has already been preserved at the exit entry point.
- **Stop action**: Why you stopped, what state was saved, and whether a pre-change route snapshot was retained.
- **Hypotheses ruled out**: List only what this run's records have ruled out; leave blank if nothing has been ruled out.
- **Resume point**: Which step to continue from, rather than a vague "continue monitoring".

Do not record "not reproduced" as "no issue". If the next person has no choice but to start over, clearly state the reason: the original input is missing, too many changes were made to the samples, the first post-recovery record is missing, or it has not yet been confirmed whether the two states belong to the same object.

## Addendum to Earlier Records

Early records treated the IPv6 extension header and dedicated DNS chain as fixed stopping points. These terms can only remind the on-call engineer not to clear the state, and are not sufficient to replace the first difference in this replay. The recording approach has now changed to saving the original input and current revision first, then deciding whether to stop based on the actual sequence.

Likewise, earlier records treated "running to the end" as a necessary condition. Once the exit entry point breaks at step three, that approach no longer applies: continuing the run will mix in new states from after the breakpoint. Preserving step three, stopping the replay, and handing off to the next person are the results this failed run should leave behind.

Related navigation: VPND-004 is used to reorder the page timeline and current revision; VPND-007 retains the original-input replay and the exit breakpoint at step three; VPND-008 records the pre-change route snapshot; VPND-011 sets constraints on the first post-recovery record; VPND-015 is used to check objects with two states. For comparison records in which only the current revision changes, see DOC-42.

versions.body:
# Native Build Image Rotation Deviation Postmortem

Within the native build image rotation window, the visible result of the native build did not match the original plan. When this record was written, it could be confirmed only that the deviation occurred during the rotation window; it could not be confirmed whether it was caused by the rotation contents, rotation timing, build inputs, or a transient difference in the execution environment. After temporary recovery, the result became visible again, but that action did not turn the cause into a known fact.

## Incident sequence

When the deviation was first found, the on-call assessment initially pointed to image rotation itself. This assessment came from temporal overlap, not from build evidence that had already been verified. The investigation therefore started by asking "whether the switch had taken effect," rather than immediately treating all native build entry points as failed. This earlier assessment is retained here because it explains the initial handling scope and prevents hindsight from rewriting the state of knowledge too cleanly when only successful results are reviewed.

We then traced back the call names near `mobile/src/main/rust/vpnhotspotd/build.rs`: `build`, `run`, and `rerun`. This was the entry point found at the time. The trace-back showed that the issue had been traced from here, but it did not narrow the deviation to a particular change or prove that the issue permanently belonged to this file. We did not continue outward to piece together a complete build chain because the on-site material supported only this local entry point.

The failed run was kept during the trace-back. It was not a temporary marker that a later successful result overwrote; it was an observation that actually occurred during the window. After the targeted rerun passed, the earlier broad assessment—"all native runs at the same time could not complete"—no longer held. The successful rerun did not erase the first failure. The two records respectively show that a run once deviated and that a run of the same target type could later proceed; they cannot be collapsed into a single conclusion.

Temporary recovery made build results available to the on-call shift again. The purpose of recovery was to make the result visible and usable again, not to confirm that the rotation had been fixed. At the end of the incident handling, the recovery time was not recorded as the time the root cause was confirmed; at that point, it was still unknown why the first run and subsequent rerun differed. This distinction is easy to lose in retrospect, especially if only the successful CI job is retained or only the final output is cited.

## Impact scope

The deviation affected the entry point for judging native build status during the rotation window. Originally, one run's result could be used directly as a signal of whether the rotation was progressing as planned; once a failure and then a passing targeted rerun appeared, no single result could represent the entire window. To know what happened before and after recovery, the failed run, successful rerun, and their temporal order must all be visible.

Existing records do not show that the issue extended to all build entry points, and there is no material indicating that every image rotation reproduces the same behavior. Accordingly, normal runs outside the window were not included in the incident scope, and a single-window deviation was not escalated into a failure of the entire native build path. This is a narrow scope determination; it does not mean other entry points have been proven never to be affected. It reflects only what could be confirmed on site.

There was a statement that made it easier to close out the on-call response: the targeted rerun passed, so the earlier failure could be treated as transient noise during the switch. This statement was not removed because it did help restore visible results; it cannot support attribution. If the earlier failure were removed from the material, a reviewer would see only "it passed later" and incorrectly assume that no deviation had ever occurred during the window; if only the failure remained, they would miss the fact that the same entry point could later complete.

## Retained material

The on-site record retained the correspondence between the failed run and the subsequent rerun, as well as the packet fixture and decoded fields. The former was used to reconstruct which of the two observations came first; the latter two were used to verify the packet content handled at the time. What is preserved here is observation material, not an already-organized causal chain; packet fixture and decoded fields do not independently prove the image rotation state, and the path around build.rs does not independently establish ownership of the issue.

When reviewing the material, first assess the failed run and its corresponding targeted rerun together, then check whether the packet fixture and decoded fields still line up. Do not replace the original failed record with the successful rerun, and do not infer from the failure output alone that the entire window was unusable. Both runs occurred on site; the point of preserving them is precisely to keep the recovery result and the original deviation visible together.

The control point added this time is recorded verbatim:

> Keep a failed native run visible when a targeted rerun passes; the two observations answer different questions.

The rule is about the order of recording and assessment; it does not require every failure to be escalated into an image incident. Once the targeted rerun passes, the initial failure should still remain in the window record; recovery only says that a later run yielded a result again. This separates "a deviation occurred" from "it later passed" and avoids presenting an unexplained difference as a completed fix.

## Unresolved

The direct cause of the deviation remains unknown. Existing material has not confirmed whether the initial failure came from the rotation contents, rotation timing, build inputs, or a transient difference in the execution environment, nor has it established a credible order among these possibilities. A trace-back around `build.rs` and the nearby `build`, `run`, and `rerun` left only entry clues; it did not produce a diff, log, or call relationship sufficient to support a root-cause judgment.

Likewise, it has not been confirmed why the targeted rerun passed. It may simply indicate that the conditions for the later run were different, or it may only have temporarily bypassed a deviation that could not be reproduced earlier; the existing record cannot choose between these two explanations. Temporary recovery did not change this unknown, so the recovery action cannot be recorded as a validated fix.

If another window of this kind occurs, first establish the correspondence among the failed run, subsequent targeted rerun, packet fixture, and decoded fields, and preserve each one's place in the timeline. Only then will subsequent material have a chance to distinguish a per-run difference from the effect of the rotation itself. This page remains the historical record of this window and cannot replace a build assessment formed later.
